chapters.title: אוֹז הַנּוֹרָא נֶחְשָׂף
chapters.orig_title: The Discovery of Oz, the Terrible

s.line: The four travelers walked up to the great gate of Emerald City and rang the bell.
s.note: נִגַּשׁ אֶל = "went up to, approached". צִלְצֵל בְּ־ = "rang (a bell)"; note the בְּ־. In everyday speech צִלְצֵל also means "to phone": צִלְצַלְתִּי אֵלֶיךָ אֶתְמוֹל (I called you yesterday).

s.line: After ringing several times, it was opened by the same Guardian of the Gates they had met before.
s.note: אוֹתוֹ before a noun means "the same": אוֹתוֹ שׁוֹמֵר (the same guard), בְּאוֹתוֹ זְמַן (at the same time), אוֹתוֹ דָּבָר (the same thing). The feminine is אוֹתָהּ: אוֹתָהּ יַלְדָּה. Hebrew turns Baum's passive ("it was opened by") into an active sentence, which sounds more natural.

s.line: “What! are you back again?” he asked, in surprise.
“Do you not see us?” answered the Scarecrow.

w: הַמְּכַשֵּׁפָה הָרָעָה מֵהַמַּעֲרָב|the Wicked Witch of the West
s.line: “But I thought you had gone to visit the Wicked Witch of the West.”
s.note: בִּקֵּר אֵצֶל = visit a person (lit. "at someone's place"); a place takes בְּ־: בִּקַּרְנוּ בְּיָפוֹ. The same verb also means "to criticize", so מְבַקֵּר is both a visitor and a critic, and בִּקֹּרֶת is criticism.

s.line: “We did visit her,” said the Scarecrow.

w: נָתְנָה לָכֶם לָלֶכֶת|let you go|~lit. gave to you to go
s.line: “And she let you go again?” asked the man, in wonder.
s.note: נָתַן לְ־ + infinitive = "let, allow": תֵּן לִי לַעֲבֹר (let me pass), הִיא לֹא נוֹתֶנֶת לוֹ לִישֹׁן (she doesn't let him sleep). תַּדְהֵמָה = astonishment, stronger than הַפְתָּעָה.

w: לֹא הָיְתָה לָהּ בְּרֵרָה|she had no choice|~idiom
s.line: “She could not help it, for she is melted,” explained the Scarecrow.
s.note: לֹא הָיְתָה לָהּ בְּרֵרָה = "she had no choice", the past of the very common אֵין בְּרֵרָה (there's no choice). נָמַס (nif'al) = "melted" by itself, as ice melts; its hif'il partner הֵמֵס = "melted (something)", which comes next.

s.line: “Melted! Well, that is good news, indeed,” said the man.
s.note: חֲדָשׁוֹת ("news") is plural in Hebrew, so it takes אֵלֶּה and טוֹבוֹת. הַחֲדָשׁוֹת is also the news broadcast: רָאִיתָ אֶת הַחֲדָשׁוֹת?

s.line: “Who melted her?”
“It was Dorothy,” said the Lion gravely.

w: אֱלֹהִים אַדִּירִים|good gracious|~idiom: lit. mighty God
s.line: “Good gracious!” exclaimed the man, and he bowed very low indeed before her.
s.note: אֱלֹהִים אַדִּירִים! is an everyday exclamation of shock, like "good heavens!". קָד קִידָה is the verb + noun pattern you know; a "low" bow is עֲמֻקָּה, "deep".

s.line: Then he led them into his little room and locked the spectacles from the great box on all their eyes,
s.note: נָעַל = "locked" (מַנְעוּל = a lock). The same verb is used for putting on shoes: הִיא נָעֲלָה נַעֲלַיִם (she put on shoes), and נַעַל = shoe.

s.line: just as he had done before.
Afterward they passed on through the gate into the Emerald City.

w: מִשּׁוֹמֵר הַשְּׁעָרִים|from the Guardian of the Gates
הַמְּכַשֵּׁפָה הָרָעָה מֵהַמַּעֲרָב|the Wicked Witch of the West
s.line: When the people heard from the Guardian of the Gates that Dorothy had melted the Wicked Witch of the West, they all gathered around the travelers and followed them in a great crowd to the Palace of Oz.
s.note: הִתְאַסְּפוּ is hitpa'el, "gathered (themselves) together". Its pa'al partner אָסַף needs an object: אָסַף בּוּלִים (collected stamps). A public assembly is an אֲסֵפָה. Note also הָלַךְ אַחֲרֵי = "followed".

w: הַחַיָּל עִם הַזָּקָן הַיָּרֹק|the soldier with the green whiskers
s.line: The soldier with the green whiskers was still on guard before the door, but he let them in at once,
s.note: הִכְנִיס (hif'il) = "brought in, let in", the causative of נִכְנַס (went in). עָמַד עַל הַמִּשְׁמָר = "stood guard"; in modern use it also means "to be on the alert": צָרִיךְ לַעֲמֹד עַל הַמִּשְׁמָר.

s.line: and they were again met by the beautiful green girl,
who showed each of them to their old rooms at once, so they might rest until the Great Oz was ready to receive them.
s.note: מוּכָן ("ready") is a hof'al participle: "prepared", the passive of הֵכִין (prepared). כְּדֵי שֶׁ ("so that") takes the future, even in a past story: כְּדֵי שֶׁיּוּכְלוּ. קִבֵּל is both "to get" and "to receive (guests)"; a reception is קַבָּלַת פָּנִים.

w: דָּאַג שֶׁ|made sure that|~idiom: lit. worried that
s.line: The soldier had the news carried straight to Oz that Dorothy and the other travelers had come back again, after destroying the Wicked Witch;
s.note: דָּאַג שֶׁ + future = "made sure that, saw to it that". דָּאַג alone means "worried": אַל תִּדְאַג (don't worry); דָּאַג לְ־ = "took care of": הִיא דּוֹאֶגֶת לַיְּלָדִים. יְדִיעָה is a news item, the word you'll see in the papers.

s.line: but Oz made no reply.
They thought the Great Wizard would send for them at once, but he did not.
s.note: After "thought that", Hebrew keeps the tense of the original thought: they thought "he will call", so יִקְרָא, future. English shifts it to "would". קָרָא לְ־ = "called for, summoned"; without לְ־, קָרָא means "read".

s.line: They had no word from him the next day, nor the next, nor the next.
The waiting was tiresome and wearing,
s.note: מַתִּישׁ = "exhausting, draining", very common in speech: הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה הָיָה מַתִּישׁ. הַמְתָּנָה is the noun from הִמְתִּין (waited); a waiting room is a חֲדַר הַמְתָּנָה.

s.line: and at last they grew vexed that Oz should treat them in so poor a fashion, after sending them to undergo hardships and slavery.
s.note: הִתְיַחֵס אֶל = "treated, related to": הוּא מִתְיַחֵס אֵלֶיהָ יָפֶה (he treats her well). It also means "referred to": הַשַּׂר לֹא הִתְיַחֵס לַשְּׁאֵלָה (the minister didn't address the question), a phrase you'll often hear in the news. כָּעַס עַל כָּךְ שֶׁ = "was angry that".

s.line: So the Scarecrow at last asked the green girl to take another message to Oz,
s.note: בִּקֵּשׁ מִ־ = "asked (someone) for something / to do something"; a question is שָׁאַל, a request is בִּקֵּשׁ. מָסַר = "passed on, delivered", as in תִּמְסֹר לוֹ דְּרִישַׁת שָׁלוֹם (give him my regards).

s.line: saying if he did not let them in to see him at once they would call the Winged Monkeys to help them, and find out whether he kept his promises or not.
s.note: נֶאֱמַר is the nif'al (passive) of אָמַר: "it was said". You'll meet it in official language: בַּהוֹדָעָה נֶאֱמַר שֶׁ... (the statement said that…). קִיֵּם הַבְטָחָה = "kept a promise"; the pi'el קִיֵּם means "fulfilled, carried out" (also "held": קִיֵּם פְּגִישָׁה).

s.line: When the Wizard was given this message he was so frightened that he sent word for them to come to the Throne Room at four minutes after nine o’clock the next morning.
s.note: נִבְהַל = "got scared", a nif'al with active meaning; בֶּהָלָה = panic. Clock times are simply "hour + minutes": בְּתֵשַׁע וְאַרְבַּע דַּקּוֹת = 9:04, בְּתֵשַׁע וָחֵצִי = 9:30. הוֹדִיעַ (hif'il of the root "know") = "informed, let know"; הוֹדָעָה = message.

s.line: He had once met the Winged Monkeys in the Land of the West, and he did not wish to meet them again.

w: לַיְלָה לָבָן|a sleepless night|~idiom: lit. a white night
s.line: The four travelers passed a sleepless night,
s.note: לַיְלָה לָבָן, "a white night", is the everyday idiom for a night without sleep: הָיָה לִי לַיְלָה לָבָן. בִּלָּה = "spent (time)", and also "had a good time": בִּלִּינוּ בַּיָּם; a night out is a בִּלּוּי.

s.line: each thinking of the gift Oz had promised to bestow on him.
s.note: הֶעֱנִיק = "granted, awarded", a higher-register word for "gave", common in the news: הֶעֱנִיקוּ לָהּ פְּרָס (she was awarded a prize).

s.line: Dorothy fell asleep only once,
and then she dreamed she was in Kansas, where Aunt Em was telling her how glad she was to have her little girl at home again.
s.note: The dream is told in the present (שֶׁהִיא בְּקַנְזָס, אוֹמֶרֶת) because Hebrew keeps the tense of what she "saw" in the dream. נִרְדַּם = "fell asleep", a nif'al with active meaning; an anesthetic is a חֹמֶר הַרְדָּמָה.

w: הַחַיָּל עִם הַזָּקָן הַיָּרֹק|the green-whiskered soldier
s.line: Promptly at nine o’clock the next morning the green-whiskered soldier came to them,
and four minutes later they all went into the Throne Room of the Great Oz.
s.note: When a sentence opens with a time phrase, the verb often comes before the subject: לְמָחֳרָת בָּא הַחַיָּל, אַחַר כָּךְ נִכְנְסוּ כֻּלָּם. כֵּס is the formal word for a throne; כִּסֵּא is an ordinary chair.

s.line: Of course each one of them expected to see the Wizard in the shape he had taken before,
s.note: צִפָּה לְ־ = "expected"; צִפִּיּוֹת = expectations: הָיוּ לִי צִפִּיּוֹת גְּבוֹהוֹת. דְּמוּת = "figure, form", and also a character in a book or film.

s.line: and all were greatly surprised when they looked about and saw no one at all in the room.
s.note: הֻפְתְּעוּ is hof'al, the passive of the hif'il הִפְתִּיעַ (surprised someone): הַמְּסִבָּה הִפְתִּיעָה אוֹתָהּ → הִיא הֻפְתְּעָה. The participle מֻפְתָּע = "surprised".

s.line: They kept close to the door and closer to one another,
s.note: נִצְמַד לְ־ = "clung to, kept close to"; צָמוּד = "attached, right next to". זֶה לָזֶה = "to one another", and with other prepositions זֶה עִם זֶה, זֶה אֶת זֶה.

s.line: for the stillness of the empty room was more dreadful than any of the forms they had seen Oz take.
Presently they heard a solemn Voice, that seemed to come from somewhere near the top of the great dome, and it said:
s.note: נִשְׁמַע = "sounded", the hearing twin of נִרְאֶה (looked): זֶה נִשְׁמָע טוֹב (that sounds good). The everyday greeting מָה נִשְׁמָע? is literally "what is heard?", i.e. "what's new?". כָּלְשֶׁהוּ = "some, any (at all)": בְּמָקוֹם כָּלְשֶׁהוּ.

w: אוֹז הַגָּדוֹל וְהַנּוֹרָא|Oz, the Great and Terrible
s.line: “I am Oz, the Great and Terrible.
Why do you seek me?”
They looked again in every part of the room,
and then, seeing no one, Dorothy asked, “Where are you?”
“I am everywhere,” answered the Voice, “but to the eyes of common mortals I am invisible.
s.note: בִּלְתִּי + participle or adjective = "un-, in-": בִּלְתִּי נִרְאֶה (invisible, "not seen"), בִּלְתִּי אֶפְשָׁרִי (impossible), בִּלְתִּי מֻכָּר (unknown). בְּנֵי תְּמוּתָה = "mortals", from מֵת (die); בֶּן אָדָם is just "a person".

s.line: I will now seat myself upon my throne, that you may converse with me.”
Indeed, the Voice seemed just then to come straight from the throne itself;
s.note: עַצְמוֹ after a noun = "itself": הַכֵּס עַצְמוֹ (the throne itself), הָעִיר עַצְמָהּ. The same word gives בְּעַצְמִי (by myself).

s.line: so they walked toward it and stood in a row while Dorothy said:
“We have come to claim our promise, O Oz.”
s.note: דָּרַשׁ = "demanded, claimed"; דְּרִישָׁה = a demand, a word you'll hear in every news story about strikes and negotiations. דָּרוּשׁ (pa'ul) = "needed, wanted": דָּרוּשׁ מֶלְצַר (waiter wanted).

s.line: “What promise?” asked Oz.
“You promised to send me back to Kansas when the Wicked Witch was destroyed,” said the girl.
s.note: תֻּשְׁמַד = "will be destroyed", the hof'al (passive) of the hif'il הִשְׁמִיד (destroyed). Hebrew uses the future here, since at the time of the promise the destruction was still to come.

s.line: “And you promised to give me brains,” said the Scarecrow.
“And you promised to give me a heart,” said the Tin Woodman.
“And you promised to give me courage,” said the Cowardly Lion.
“Is the Wicked Witch really destroyed?” asked the Voice,
and Dorothy thought it trembled a little.
s.note: נִדְמֶה לִי = "it seems to me, I think", very common in polite speech: נִדְמֶה לִי שֶׁנִּפְגַּשְׁנוּ (I think we've met). In the past: הָיָה נִדְמֶה לָהּ. A yes/no question needs no special word: הִיא בֶּאֱמֶת הֻשְׁמְדָה? is a question only by intonation.

s.line: “Yes,” she answered, “I melted her with a bucket of water.”

w: אוֹי וַאֲבוֹי|dear me|~idiom: oh and alas
s.line: “Dear me,” said the Voice, “how sudden!
Well, come to me tomorrow, for I must have time to think it over.”
s.note: אוֹי וַאֲבוֹי is a half-joking "oh dear!"; וַאֲבוֹי is old-fashioned, but the pair survives in speech. פִּתְאֹמִי = "sudden", the adjective from פִּתְאֹם (suddenly).

w: הָיָה לְךָ|you had|~lit. there was to you
s.line: “You’ve had plenty of time already,” said the Tin Woodman angrily.
s.note: בְּ־ + noun is the usual way to make an adverb of manner: בְּכַעַס (angrily), בְּשֶׁקֶט (quietly), בְּהַפְתָּעָה (in surprise). מַסְפִּיק is a hif'il participle, "suffices", used as "enough": מַסְפִּיק! (that's enough!).

s.line: “We shan’t wait a day longer,” said the Scarecrow.
“You must keep your promises to us!” exclaimed Dorothy.
s.note: חַיָּב = "must, obliged"; it agrees with the subject: הִיא חַיֶּבֶת, אֲנַחְנוּ חַיָּבִים. It also means "owes": אַתָּה חַיָּב לִי כֶּסֶף. A promise is "given" in Hebrew: נָתַן הַבְטָחָה.

s.line: The Lion thought it might be as well to frighten the Wizard,
s.note: כְּדַאי = "it's worth it, it's a good idea": כְּדַאי לְךָ לָבוֹא (you'd better come), לֹא כְּדַאי (better not). הִפְחִיד (hif'il) = "frightened (someone)", the causative of פָּחַד (was afraid).

s.line: so he gave a large, loud roar, which was so fierce and dreadful that Toto jumped away from him in alarm and tipped over the screen that stood in a corner.
s.note: שָׁאַג שְׁאָגָה is the verb + noun pattern again. הִפִּיל (hif'il) = "made fall, knocked over", from נָפַל (fell); the נ of the root disappears into the dagesh. פַּרְגּוֹד = a folding screen or partition.

s.line: As it fell with a crash they looked that way,
and the next moment all of them were filled with wonder.
For they saw, standing in just the spot the screen had hidden, a little old man, with a bald head and a wrinkled face, who seemed to be as much surprised as they were.
s.note: מְקֻמָּט = "wrinkled", a pu'al participle (passive of קִמֵּט, crumpled); קֶמֶט = a wrinkle. פָּנִים is plural in form, so its adjective is plural too: פָּנִים מְקֻמָּטוֹת. כְּמוֹתָם = "like them" (כְּמוֹנִי, כְּמוֹךָ…).

s.line: The Tin Woodman, raising his axe, rushed toward the little man and cried out, “Who are you?”
s.note: זִנֵּק = "leaped, sprang forward"; in the news, prices זִנְּקוּ (shot up), and a race starts with a זִנּוּק. לְעֵבֶר = "toward", a bit more written than אֶל.

w: אוֹז הַגָּדוֹל וְהַנּוֹרָא|Oz, the Great and Terrible
s.line: “I am Oz, the Great and Terrible,” said the little man, in a trembling voice.
“But don’t strike me—please don’t—and I’ll do anything you want me to.”
s.note: אַל + future = "don't!": אַל תַּכֶּה, אַל תִּדְאַג, אַל תְּדַבֵּר. לֹא + future is a flat "you won't / you shall not". הִכָּה (hif'il, root נ־כ־ה) = "hit, struck"; in the future תַּכֶּה the נ of the root has dropped out, leaving only the dagesh in the כּ.

w: וּבְמַפַּח נֶפֶשׁ|and in dismay|~idiom: bitter disappointment
s.line: Our friends looked at him in surprise and dismay.
s.note: מַפַּח נֶפֶשׁ = "bitter disappointment, dismay", a higher-register phrase that journalists like: הַתּוֹצָאָה הָיְתָה מַפַּח נֶפֶשׁ (the result was a letdown). Note הִבִּיט בְּ־ = "looked at".

s.line: “I thought Oz was a great Head,” said Dorothy.
s.note: Again no change of tense after "thought": חָשַׁבְתִּי שֶׁאוֹז הוּא... = "I thought Oz was…". Here הוּא works as "is", linking the subject to what it is.

s.line: “And I thought Oz was a lovely Lady,” said the Scarecrow.
“And I thought Oz was a terrible Beast,” said the Tin Woodman.
“And I thought Oz was a Ball of Fire,” exclaimed the Lion.
“No, you are all wrong,” said the little man meekly.
s.note: טוֹעֶה = "mistaken, wrong" (of a person): אַתָּה טוֹעֶה (you're wrong). The noun is טָעוּת (a mistake), which comes up again below. כֻּלְּכֶם = "all of you" (כֻּלָּנוּ, כֻּלָּם).

w: הֶעֱמַדְתִּי פָּנִים|I pretended|~idiom: lit. I set up a face
s.line: “I have been making believe.”
s.note: הֶעֱמִיד פָּנִים = "pretended, made believe", a fixed everyday phrase: הוּא מַעֲמִיד פָּנִים שֶׁהוּא יָשֵׁן (he's pretending to be asleep).

s.line: “Making believe!” cried Dorothy.
“Are you not a Great Wizard?”
“Hush, my dear,” he said.
“Don’t speak so loud, or you will be overheard—and I should be ruined.
s.note: יִשְׁמְעוּ אוֹתָךְ ("they will hear you") with no subject is the everyday Hebrew way to say "you will be heard": the 3rd person plural stands in for an English passive, like אוֹמְרִים שֶׁ... (it is said that…). אָבוּד = "lost, done for"; הָלַךְ לְאִבּוּד = "got lost".

s.line: I’m supposed to be a Great Wizard.”
s.note: אָמוּר + infinitive = "supposed to", literally "said (to be)", a pa'ul participle of אָמַר. It is everywhere in speech: הָאוֹטוֹבּוּס אָמוּר לְהַגִּיעַ (the bus is supposed to come), הִיא אֲמוּרָה לָדַעַת.

s.line: “And aren’t you?” she asked.
“Not a bit of it, my dear;
I’m just a common man.”
s.note: סְתָם = "just, merely, for no reason": סְתָם אָדָם (just some guy), סְתָם כָּכָה (just because). Alone, סְתָם! means "just kidding!". מַמָּשׁ לֹא = "not at all, absolutely not".

s.line: “You’re more than that,” said the Scarecrow, in a grieved tone; “you’re a humbug.”

w: מָצָא חֵן בְּעֵינָיו|pleased him|~idiom: lit. found grace in his eyes
s.line: “Exactly so!” declared the little man, rubbing his hands together as if it pleased him.
s.note: מָצָא חֵן בְּעֵינֵי = "pleased, was liked by", the standard way to say "I like it": זֶה מוֹצֵא חֵן בְּעֵינַי. הִכְרִיז = "declared, announced", a news word: הַמֶּמְשָׁלָה הִכְרִיזָה / הַכְרָזָה.

s.line: “I am a humbug.”
“But this is terrible,” said the Tin Woodman.
“How shall I ever get my heart?”
s.note: אֵי פַּעַם = "ever": הָיִיתָ אֵי פַּעַם בְּאֵילַת? (have you ever been to Eilat?). Don't confuse it with אַף פַּעַם, which goes with לֹא and means "never".

s.line: “Or I my courage?” asked the Lion.
“Or I my brains?” wailed the Scarecrow, wiping the tears from his eyes with his coat sleeve.
s.note: נִגֵּב = "wiped, dried"; a towel is a מַגֶּבֶת, from the same root. יִלֵּל = "wailed, howled", also used for a dog or the wind; an air-raid siren is said to לְיַלֵּל.

s.line: “My dear friends,” said Oz, “I pray you not to speak of these little things.
s.note: הִתְחַנֵּן (hitpa'el) = "begged, pleaded", from the root of חֵן (grace) and חֲנִינָה (a pardon). חֲבֵרַי ("my friends") is a fixed possessive form, natural in a direct address like this one.

w: נֶחְשַׂפְתִּי|I have been found out|!nif'al · ח־שׂ־ף
s.line: Think of me, and the terrible trouble I’m in at being found out.”
s.note: נֶחְשַׂף = "was exposed, was found out", the nif'al (passive) of חָשַׂף (exposed); it gives the chapter its title. In the news, a חֲשִׂיפָה is an exposé. תַּחְשְׁבוּ: in speech the future form is the usual command; the literary imperative is חִשְׁבוּ.

s.line: “Doesn’t anyone else know you’re a humbug?” asked Dorothy.
“No one knows it but you four—and myself,” replied Oz.
s.note: אַרְבַּעְתְּכֶם = "the four of you", a number with a possessive ending: שְׁנֵינוּ (the two of us), שְׁלָשְׁתָּם (the three of them). הֵשִׁיב = "replied", more formal than עָנָה; it is the hif'il of שָׁב (returned), so it is literally "gave back (an answer)".

s.line: “I have fooled everyone so long that I thought I should never be found out.
s.note: רִמָּה (pi'el) = "fooled, cheated", and רַמַּאי (humbug, con man) comes from the same root; רַמָּאוּת = fraud. יְגַלּוּ אוֹתִי is again the subjectless "they" standing in for "I will be found out".

s.line: It was a great mistake my ever letting you into the Throne Room.

w: בְּדֶרֶךְ כְּלָל|usually|~idiom: lit. in a general way
s.line: Usually I will not see even my subjects, and so they believe I am something terrible.”
s.note: לֹא מוּכָן + infinitive = "not willing to, refuse to": הוּא לֹא מוּכָן לְדַבֵּר. נְתִינִים = "subjects" of a ruler; in modern use נָתִין is a foreign national, as in נָתִין זָר, and נְתִינוּת = citizenship.

s.line: “But, I don’t understand,” said Dorothy, in bewilderment.

w: אֵיךְ זֶה שֶׁ|how is it that|~idiom
s.line: “How was it that you appeared to me as a great Head?”
s.note: אֵיךְ זֶה שֶׁ...? = "how come…?", very common in speech: אֵיךְ זֶה שֶׁאַתָּה כָּאן? (how come you're here?). הוֹפִיעַ = "appeared", also "performed (on stage)"; a show is an הוֹפָעָה.

s.line: “That was one of my tricks,” answered Oz.
s.note: תַּרְגִּיל = "trick, ruse", and also "exercise" (homework, gym) and a military "drill". Context decides: תַּרְגִּיל בְּמָתֵמָטִיקָה is a math exercise.

s.line: “Step this way, please, and I will tell you all about it.”
He led the way to a small chamber in the rear of the Throne Room, and they all followed him.
He pointed to one corner,
s.note: הִצְבִּיעַ עַל = "pointed at"; without עַל it is also "voted" or "raised a hand in class": הִצְבַּעְתִּי בַּבְּחִירוֹת. The finger used for pointing is the אֶצְבַּע. אַחַת הַפִּנּוֹת = "one of the corners", with the number before a definite plural.

w: וְהָיוּ לוֹ|and it had|~lit. there were to it
s.line: in which lay the great Head, made out of many thicknesses of paper, and with a carefully painted face.
s.note: Three passive forms in one sentence: מֻנָּח (hof'al of הִנִּיחַ, put down) = "placed, lying"; עָשׂוּי (pa'ul) = "made of": עָשׂוּי מֵעֵץ; and צֻיְּרוּ, the pu'al past of צִיֵּר (painted): הַפָּנִים צֻיְּרוּ = "the face was painted".

s.line: “This I hung from the ceiling by a wire,” said Oz.
s.note: Putting the object first (אֶת זֶה תָּלִיתִי) stresses it, as in Baum's "This I hung". תָּלָה = "hung"; the pa'ul תָּלוּי = "hanging", and also "depends": זֶה תָּלוּי בְּךָ (it's up to you).

s.line: “I stood behind the screen and pulled a thread, to make the eyes move and the mouth open.”
s.note: מָשַׁךְ בְּ־ = "pulled on": מָשַׁךְ בַּחֶבֶל. Without בְּ־, מָשַׁךְ can mean "attracted" or "withdrew (money)". יִפָּתַח is nif'al with an active sense here, "would open (by itself)".

s.line: “But how about the voice?” she inquired.
s.note: מָה עִם + noun = "what about …?", one of the most useful phrases in spoken Hebrew: מָה עִם הַכֶּסֶף? (what about the money?), מָה אִתְּךָ? (what's up with you?).

w: מְדַבֵּר מֵהַבֶּטֶן|a ventriloquist|~lit. one who speaks from the belly
s.line: “Oh, I am a ventriloquist,” said the little man.
s.note: Hebrew has no single everyday word for "ventriloquist"; the usual phrase is מְדַבֵּר מֵהַבֶּטֶן, "a speaker from the belly".

s.line: “I can throw the sound of my voice wherever I wish,
so that you thought it was coming out of the Head.
s.note: חָשַׁבְתְּ שֶׁהוּא יוֹצֵא: "you thought it is coming out". After verbs of thinking, saying and seeing, Hebrew keeps the tense of the original thought. English shifts it back to "was"; Hebrew does not.

s.line: Here are the other things I used to deceive you.”
s.note: הִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ בְּ־ = to use: the thing used takes בְּ, so "the things I used" becomes הַדְּבָרִים שֶׁבָּהֶם הִשְׁתַּמַּשְׁתִּי. רִמָּה (to deceive, cheat) shares its root with רַמַּאי, the humbug himself.

s.line: He showed the Scarecrow the dress and the mask he had worn when he seemed to be the lovely Lady.
s.note: הִתְחַזָּה לְ־ = to pose as, impersonate. It is common in the news: הוּא הִתְחַזָּה לְשׁוֹטֵר (he posed as a policeman); a con man is מִתְחַזֶּה.

w: לֹא הָיְתָה אֶלָּא|was nothing but|~idiom: לֹא … אֶלָּא = only
s.line: And the Tin Woodman saw that his terrible Beast was nothing but a lot of skins,
s.note: לֹא … אֶלָּא = "nothing but, only": זֶה לֹא הָיָה אֶלָּא חֲלוֹם (it was only a dream). It is a little more literary than רַק, but you will meet it often in writing.

s.line: sewn together, with slats to keep their sides out.
s.note: נִתְפַּר is the nif'al (passive) of תָּפַר (to sew): "was sewn". The noun is תְּפִירָה (sewing), and a tailor is חַיָּט.

w: וּבַאֲשֶׁר לְכַדּוּר הָאֵשׁ|and as for the Ball of Fire|~set phrase: בַּאֲשֶׁר לְ־ = as for
s.line: As for the Ball of Fire, the false Wizard had hung that also from the ceiling.
s.note: בַּאֲשֶׁר לְ־ = "as for, regarding", a written and news-register phrase. מְזֻיָּף is a pu'al participle, "forged, fake": כֶּסֶף מְזֻיָּף (counterfeit money), דַּרְכּוֹן מְזֻיָּף (a forged passport).

s.line: It was really a ball of cotton,
but when oil was poured upon it the ball burned fiercely.
s.note: כְּשֶׁיָּצְקוּ = "when they poured", with no "they" in view. Hebrew often uses a 3rd-person plural verb with no subject where English uses a passive ("oil was poured").

s.line: “Really,” said the Scarecrow, “you ought to be ashamed of yourself for being such a humbug.”
s.note: לְהִתְבַּיֵּשׁ (hitpa'el) = to be ashamed, and also to be shy: אַל תִּתְבַּיֵּשׁ! (don't be shy!). The scolding "shame on you!" is תִּתְבַּיֵּשׁ לְךָ!

s.line: “I am—I certainly am,” answered the little man sorrowfully;
“but it was the only thing I could do.
Sit down, please, there are plenty of chairs;
s.note: שְׁבוּ is the plural imperative of יָשַׁב: שֵׁב (to a man), שְׁבִי (to a woman), שְׁבוּ (to a group). The first letter י drops out, as in לָשֶׁבֶת (to sit).

s.line: and I will tell you my story.”
So they sat down and listened while he told the following tale.
s.note: הִקְשִׁיב לְ־ = to listen to (שָׁמַע is just "to hear"). הַבָּא, "the coming one", is the normal word for "next, following": בַּשָּׁבוּעַ הַבָּא (next week), הַבָּא בַּתּוֹר! (next in line!).

s.line: “I was born in Omaha—”
s.note: נוֹלַד (was born) is the nif'al of the root י־ל־ד, the same root as יֶלֶד (child), יָלְדָה (she gave birth) and יוֹם הֻלֶּדֶת (birthday).

s.line: “Why, that isn’t very far from Kansas!” cried Dorothy.
“No, but it’s farther from here,” he said, shaking his head at her sadly.

w: מְדַבֵּר מֵהַבֶּטֶן|a ventriloquist|~lit. one who speaks from the belly
s.line: “When I grew up I became a ventriloquist,
s.note: נַעֲשָׂה is the nif'al of עָשָׂה (to do, make). It can be passive ("was made"), but here it means "became". In speech you will also hear הָפַכְתִּי לִ־ for "I became".

s.line: and at that I was very well trained by a great master.
s.note: English "I was trained" becomes active קִבַּלְתִּי הַכְשָׁרָה, "I received training". הַכְשָׁרָה is everyday job vocabulary: הַכְשָׁרָה מִקְצוֹעִית (vocational training).

s.line: I can imitate any kind of a bird or beast.”
Here he mewed so like a kitten that Toto pricked up his ears and looked everywhere to see where she was.
s.note: יִלֵּל = to wail, howl; for a cat it is the normal word for "to meow": הֶחָתוּל מְיַלֵּל. חֲתַלְתּוּל (kitten) is the diminutive of חָתוּל. לְכָל עֵבֶר = "in all directions".

w: נִמְאַס לִי|I got tired|~idiom: I got fed up
טַיַּס כַּדּוּר פּוֹרֵחַ|a balloonist|~lit. a balloon pilot
s.line: “After a time,” continued Oz, “I tired of that, and became a balloonist.”
s.note: זְמַן מָה = "some time, a while", and נִמְאַס לִי מִ־ = "I'm fed up with". טַיָּס is a pilot; טָס means "to fly", as in טַסְתִּי לְאֵילַת (I flew to Eilat).

s.line: “What is that?” asked Dorothy.
“A man who goes up in a balloon on circus day,
s.note: מַגִּיעַ (arrives) is a hif'il participle of נ־ג־ע; the נ of the root disappears into the dagesh. The same word also means "deserves": מַגִּיעַ לְךָ! (you deserve it!).

s.line: so as to draw a crowd of people together and get them to pay to see the circus,” he explained.
s.note: גָּרַם לְ־ + infinitive = "to make / get someone to do": הוּא גָּרַם לִי לִצְחֹק (he made me laugh). With a noun it means "to cause": גָּרַם נֵזֶק (caused damage).

s.line: “Oh,” she said, “I know.”
“Well, one day I went up in a balloon and the ropes got twisted,
s.note: הִסְתַּבֵּךְ (hitpa'el) = to get tangled, and in everyday speech "to get into trouble": הוּא הִסְתַּבֵּךְ עִם הַמִּשְׁטָרָה. In hitpa'el the ת swaps places with a first root letter ס: not הִתְסַבֵּךְ but הִסְתַּבֵּךְ.

s.line: so that I couldn’t come down again.
It went way up above the clouds,
so far that a current of air struck it and carried it many, many miles away.
s.note: פָּגַע בְּ־ = to hit, strike; the target takes בְּ. It also means "to hurt, offend": לֹא רָצִיתִי לִפְגֹּעַ בְּךָ (I didn't mean to hurt you).

s.line: For a day and a night I traveled through the air,
and on the morning of the second day I awoke and found the balloon floating over a strange and beautiful country.
s.note: מְרַחֵף = hovering, floating in the air. The same root gives two modern words: רַחְפָן (a drone) and רַחֶפֶת (a hovercraft).

s.line: “It came down gradually, and I was not hurt a bit.
s.note: נִפְגַּע is the nif'al (passive) of פָּגַע: "was hit, was hurt". It is in nearly every news report of an accident: שְׁנֵי אֲנָשִׁים נִפְגְּעוּ (two people were injured).

s.line: But I found myself in the midst of a strange people,
who, seeing me come from the clouds, thought I was a great Wizard.
s.note: רָאוּ אוֹתִי יוֹרֵד: after רָאָה, a present participle describes what was seen happening, like English "saw me coming down".

s.line: Of course I let them think so,
s.note: נָתַן לְ־ + infinitive = "to let someone do": תֵּן לִי לַעֲבֹר (let me pass), הִיא לֹא נוֹתֶנֶת לִי לָלֶכֶת (she won't let me go).

s.line: because they were afraid of me, and promised to do anything I wished them to.
“Just to amuse myself, and keep the good people busy, I ordered them to build this City, and my Palace;
s.note: צִוָּה עַל = to order someone; the person ordered takes עַל. לְבַדֵּר gives בִּדּוּר (entertainment), and לְהַעֲסִיק also means "to employ": הַחֶבְרָה מַעֲסִיקָה מֵאָה עוֹבְדִים.

s.line: and they did it all willingly and well.
Then I thought, as the country was so green and beautiful, I would call it the Emerald City;
s.note: קָרָא לְ־ + name = "to name, call": קָרְאוּ לוֹ דָּן (they named him Dan). Without לְ the verb means "to read" or "to call out".

s.line: and to make the name fit better I put green spectacles on all the people,
s.note: מַתְאִים = suitable, fitting, and in daily life "convenient": זֶה לֹא מַתְאִים לִי (that doesn't suit me / that's not a good time for me).

s.line: so that everything they saw was green.”
“But isn’t everything here green?” asked Dorothy.
s.note: הַאִם marks a yes/no question. It is common in writing; in speech the voice usually does the job, and הַאִם sounds a little formal.

s.line: “No more than in any other city,” replied Oz;
“but when you wear green spectacles, why of course everything you see looks green to you.
s.note: Glasses are not "worn" with לָבַשׁ: Hebrew says הִרְכִּיב מִשְׁקָפַיִם. The plural participle with no subject (מַרְכִּיבִים, רוֹאִים) is the general "you, one".

s.line: The Emerald City was built a great many years ago,
s.note: נִבְנָה (fem. נִבְנְתָה) is the nif'al passive of בָּנָה (to build). "X years ago" is לִפְנֵי X שָׁנִים, with לִפְנֵי placed first.

s.line: for I was a young man when the balloon brought me here, and I am a very old man now.
But my people have worn green glasses on their eyes so long that most of them think it really is an Emerald City,
s.note: "Have worn … so long" is present tense in Hebrew, מַרְכִּיבִים, because they still wear them: אֲנִי גָּר כָּאן עֶשֶׂר שָׁנִים = "I have lived here for ten years". רֻבָּם = most of them (רֹב + "them").

s.line: and it certainly is a beautiful place,
abounding in jewels and precious metals, and every good thing that is needed to make one happy.
s.note: אֲבָנִים טוֹבוֹת, "good stones", is the standard term for gems. יָקָר means both "precious" and "expensive": הַדִּירָה יְקָרָה (the apartment is expensive).

s.line: I have been good to the people, and they like me;
but ever since this Palace was built, I have shut myself up and would not see any of them.
s.note: הִסְתַּגֵּר is the reflexive hitpa'el of סָגַר (to close): "to close oneself off, shut oneself away". It has the same ס/ת swap as הִסְתַּבֵּךְ above.

s.line: “One of my greatest fears was the Witches,
s.note: The superlative is הַ־ + adjective + בְּיוֹתֵר: הַגָּדוֹל בְּיוֹתֵר (the biggest). "Fear of" takes מִ־, just like the verb: פָּחַד מִ־.

w: לֹא הָיוּ|had no|~lit. there were not (to me)
s.line: for while I had no magical powers at all I soon found out that the Witches were really able to do wonderful things.
s.note: מְסֻגָּל לְ־ = capable of, able to. It has a pu'al form but simply means "able": הוּא לֹא מְסֻגָּל לְהוֹדוֹת בְּטָעוּת (he is incapable of admitting a mistake). מַדְהִים (amazing) is a very common everyday adjective.

s.line: There were four of them in this country, and they ruled the people who live in the North and South and East and West.
s.note: שָׁלַט בְּ־ = to rule, control; what is ruled takes בְּ. From the same root: שִׁלְטוֹן (government, regime) and שַׁלָּט (a remote control). אַרְבַּע has the feminine form because it counts מְכַשֵּׁפוֹת.

s.line: Fortunately, the Witches of the North and South were good, and I knew they would do me no harm;
s.note: לְמַזָּלִי = luckily for me; לְמַזָּלֵנוּ = luckily for us. The general "fortunately" is לְמַרְבֶּה הַמַּזָּל, and "unfortunately" is לְמַרְבֶּה הַצַּעַר.

s.line: but the Witches of the East and West were terribly wicked,
and had they not thought I was more powerful than they themselves, they would surely have destroyed me.
s.note: An unreal condition ("had they …, they would have …") uses הָיָה + participle in both halves: אִם הֵן לֹא הָיוּ חוֹשְׁבוֹת … הֵן הָיוּ מַשְׁמִידוֹת. In speech: אִם הָיִיתִי יוֹדֵעַ, הָיִיתִי בָּא (if I had known, I would have come).

w: בְּפַחַד מָוֶת|in deadly fear|~lit. in fear of death
s.line: As it was, I lived in deadly fear of them for many years;
s.note: בְּפֹעַל = "in practice, in reality", as opposed to what might have been: בְּפֹעַל הוּא לֹא עוֹבֵד כָּאן (in reality he doesn't work here). It is very frequent in the news.

w: הַמְּכַשֵּׁפָה הָרָעָה מֵהַמִּזְרָח|the Wicked Witch of the East
s.line: so you can imagine how pleased I was when I heard your house had fallen on the Wicked Witch of the East.
s.note: לְתָאֵר לְעַצְמְךָ = to imagine (lit. "to describe to yourself"). You will often hear תְּתָאֵר לְךָ! = "just imagine!"

w: שֶׁתִּפָּטְרוּ|that you would get rid|nif'al · פ־ט־ר
s.line: When you came to me, I was willing to promise anything if you would only do away with the other Witch;
s.note: מוּכָן is a hof'al participle ("prepared"), used as "ready, willing": אֲנִי מוּכָן (I'm ready). נִפְטַר מִ־ = to get rid of; on its own נִפְטַר is also the polite word for "passed away".

s.line: but, now that you have melted her, I am ashamed to say that I cannot keep my promises.”
s.note: קִיֵּם הַבְטָחָה = to keep a promise; to break one is הֵפֵר הַבְטָחָה. הֵמֵס (to melt something) is the hif'il; the ice itself נָמֵס (melts).

s.line: “I think you are a very bad man,” said Dorothy.
“Oh, no, my dear;
I’m really a very good man, but I’m a very bad Wizard, I must admit.”
s.note: Two kinds of "bad": רַע is morally bad, גָּרוּעַ is bad at something, poor quality: סֶרֶט גָּרוּעַ (a bad film). הוֹדָה בְּ־ = to admit; הוֹדָה לְ־ = to thank, the same root as תּוֹדָה.

s.line: “Can’t you give me brains?” asked the Scarecrow.
“You don’t need them.
You are learning something every day.
A baby has brains, but it doesn’t know much.
Experience is the only thing that brings knowledge,
s.note: נִסָּיוֹן = experience, the word in every job ad: דָּרוּשׁ נִסָּיוֹן (experience required). It also means "an attempt": נִסָּיוֹן לִבְרֹחַ (an escape attempt). הוּא here works as "is" between two nouns.

w: וּכְכָל|and the more|~with כָּךְ: the more … the more
s.line: and the longer you are on earth the more experience you are sure to get.”
s.note: כְּכָל שֶׁ־ …, כָּךְ … = "the more …, the more …": כְּכָל שֶׁאֲנִי לוֹמֵד, כָּךְ אֲנִי מֵבִין יוֹתֵר (the more I learn, the more I understand). צָבַר נִסָּיוֹן (to build up experience) is a fixed pair; צָבַר = to accumulate, as in צָבַר נְקֻדּוֹת (to collect points).

s.line: “That may all be true,” said the Scarecrow, “but I shall be very unhappy unless you give me brains.”
s.note: יָכוֹל לִהְיוֹת = "maybe, it could be", extremely common in speech, often as a whole answer: – הוּא יָבוֹא? – יָכוֹל לִהְיוֹת. "Unless" is simply אִם לֹא (if not).

w: בִּתְשׂוּמֶת לֵב|carefully|~lit. with attention of heart
s.line: The false Wizard looked at him carefully.
s.note: הִבִּיט בְּ־ = to look at; the thing looked at takes בְּ. תְּשׂוּמֶת לֵב = attention: שִׂים לֵב! (pay attention!) comes from the same phrase.

s.line: “Well,” he said with a sigh, “I’m not much of a magician, as I said;
s.note: אֲנָחָה = a sigh; the verb is the nif'al נֶאֱנַח (he sighed). "Not much of a …" comes out naturally as לֹא … כָּל כָּךְ: אֲנִי לֹא טַבָּח גָּדוֹל כָּל כָּךְ (I'm not much of a cook).

s.line: but if you will come to me tomorrow morning, I will stuff your head with brains.
s.note: אֲמַלֵּא לְךָ אֶת הָרֹאשׁ: "I'll fill to you the head". In speech, לְ + person often replaces a possessive when something is done to that person's body or belongings: הוּא שָׁבַר לִי אֶת הַטֵּלֵפוֹן (he broke my phone).

s.line: I cannot tell you how to use them, however;
you must find that out for yourself.”
s.note: הִצְטָרֵךְ (hitpa'el of צ־ר־ך, like צָרִיךְ) = to need to, have to. After צ the hitpa'el ת turns into ט. You will hear the future all the time: נִצְטָרֵךְ לְחַכּוֹת (we'll have to wait).

s.line: “Oh, thank you—thank you!” cried the Scarecrow.
“I’ll find a way to use them, never fear!”
s.note: אַל דְּאָגָה = "don't worry", a set phrase. As a verb: אַל תִּדְאַג (to a man), אַל תִּדְאֲגִי (to a woman).

s.line: “But how about my courage?” asked the Lion anxiously.

w: יֵשׁ לְךָ|you have|~lit. there is to you
s.line: “You have plenty of courage, I am sure,” answered Oz.
“All you need is confidence in yourself.
s.note: One root, three everyday words: בָּטוּחַ (sure; also "safe"), בִּטָּחוֹן (confidence; also "security", as in מִשְׂרַד הַבִּטָּחוֹן, the Ministry of Defense) and בִּטּוּחַ (insurance). בִּטָּחוֹן עַצְמִי = self-confidence.

s.line: There is no living thing that is not afraid when it faces danger.
s.note: עָמַד מוּל = to stand facing, to face: עָמַדְנוּ מוּל בְּעָיָה קָשָׁה (we faced a hard problem). מוּל on its own means "opposite": הַבַּיִת מוּל הַפַּארְק.

s.line: The True courage is in facing danger when you are afraid,

w: יֵשׁ לְךָ|you have|~lit. there is to you
s.line: and that kind of courage you have in plenty.”
s.note: בְּשֶׁפַע = in abundance, plenty of. The noun שֶׁפַע = abundance, and שׁוֹפֵעַ = overflowing, abundant.

w: יֵשׁ לִי|I have|~lit. there is to me
s.line: “Perhaps I have, but I’m scared just the same,” said the Lion.
s.note: בְּכָל זֹאת = "nevertheless, all the same", very common: הָיָה קַר, אֲבָל יָצָאנוּ בְּכָל זֹאת (it was cold, but we went out anyway).

s.line: “I shall really be very unhappy unless you give me the sort of courage that makes one forget he is afraid.”
“Very well, I will give you that sort of courage tomorrow,” replied Oz.
s.note: In the future of נָתַן the first נ drops and leaves a dagesh in the ת: אֶתֵּן, תִּתֵּן, יִתֵּן.

s.line: “How about my heart?” asked the Tin Woodman.

w: בְּקֶשֶׁר לְזֶה|as for that|~lit. in connection to this
s.line: “Why, as for that,” answered Oz, “I think you are wrong to want a heart.
s.note: בְּקֶשֶׁר לְ־ = "regarding, about", the everyday version of בַּאֲשֶׁר לְ־: יֵשׁ לִי שְׁאֵלָה בְּקֶשֶׁר לַשִּׁעוּר. טוֹעֶה = mistaken; טָעוּת = a mistake.

s.line: It makes most people unhappy.

w: לוּ רַק יָדַעְתָּ|if you only knew|~idiom
יֵשׁ לְךָ מַזָּל|you are lucky|~lit. there is luck to you
שֶׁאֵין לְךָ|that you have no|~lit. that there is not to you
s.line: If you only knew it, you are in luck not to have a heart.”
s.note: לוּ רַק יָדַעְתָּ = "if only you knew", a set phrase. יֵשׁ לְךָ מַזָּל = you're lucky; the opposite is אֵין לִי מַזָּל (I have no luck).

s.line: “That must be a matter of opinion,” said the Tin Woodman.
s.note: עִנְיָן שֶׁל = "a matter of". The everyday fixed phrase is זֶה עִנְיָן שֶׁל טַעַם (it's a matter of taste).

w: מִצִּדִּי|for my part|~lit. from my side
s.line: “For my part, I will bear all the unhappiness without a murmur, if you will give me the heart.”
s.note: מִצִּדִּי = "as far as I'm concerned"; מִצִּדִּי, תַּעֲשֶׂה מָה שֶׁאַתָּה רוֹצֶה (as far as I'm concerned, do what you like). סָבַל = to suffer, bear; אֲנִי לֹא סוֹבֵל אוֹתוֹ = I can't stand him.

s.line: “Very well,” answered Oz meekly.
s.note: עֲנָוָה = humility, modesty; a humble person is עָנָו. It is a literary word, but it fits Oz's sudden new tone.

w: וְיִהְיֶה לְךָ|and you will have|~lit. there will be to you
s.line: “Come to me tomorrow and you shall have a heart.
s.note: The future of "to have" is יִהְיֶה לְ־: יִהְיֶה לְךָ לֵב (you will have a heart). As with הָיָה לְ־, the verb agrees with the thing owned: תִּהְיֶה לְךָ מְכוֹנִית, יִהְיוּ לְךָ חֲבֵרִים.

w: שֶׁאֶפְשָׁר|that I may as well|~lit. that it's possible
s.line: I have played Wizard for so many years that I may as well continue the part a little longer.”
s.note: מְשַׂחֵק = to play, and also to act on stage; an actor or player is שַׂחְקָן. תַּפְקִיד = a role, and at work "a job, position": מָה הַתַּפְקִיד שֶׁלְּךָ? (what's your position?).

s.line: “And now,” said Dorothy, “how am I to get back to Kansas?”
s.note: אָמוּר לְ־, literally "said", is the pa'ul participle of אָמַר and means "supposed to": הָאוֹטוֹבּוּס אָמוּר לְהַגִּיעַ (the bus is supposed to arrive). Dorothy uses the feminine אֲמוּרָה.

s.line: “We shall have to think about that,” replied the little man.

w: אֶל מֵעֵבֶר לַמִּדְבָּר|over the desert|~lit. to beyond the desert
s.line: “Give me two or three days to consider the matter and I’ll try to find a way to carry you over the desert.
s.note: יוֹמַיִם is the dual of יוֹם: "two days", in one word. The same ending gives שְׁבוּעַיִם (two weeks), שְׁנָתַיִם (two years) and פַּעֲמַיִם (twice). נִסָּה (to try) shares its root with נִסָּיוֹן.

w: אֶל כֻּלְּכֶם|all of you|~lit. to all of you
s.line: In the meantime you shall all be treated as my guests,
s.note: הִתְיַחֵס אֶל = to treat (someone), and also "to relate to, respond to": הוּא לֹא הִתְיַחֵס לַשְּׁאֵלָה (he didn't address the question). The noun יַחַס = attitude, treatment. No subject is named, so the 3rd-person plural verb again does the work of an English passive.

s.line: and while you live in the Palace my people will wait upon you and obey your slightest wish.
s.note: מִלֵּא מִשְׁאָלָה = to grant a wish (lit. to fill it). שֵׁרֵת = to serve; from the same root: שֵׁרוּת (service) and שֵׁרוּתִים (restrooms, lit. "services").

s.line: There is only one thing I ask in return for my help—such as it is.
s.note: בִּתְמוּרָה לְ־ = in return for, in exchange for: מָה אֲנִי מְקַבֵּל בִּתְמוּרָה? (what do I get in return?). "Such as it is" comes out as "if one can call it help".

w: לְאַף אֶחָד|to anyone|~with לֹא: to no one
s.line: You must keep my secret and tell no one I am a humbug.”
They agreed to say nothing of what they had learned,
s.note: הִסְכִּים = to agree; the noun הֶסְכֵּם (an agreement, treaty) is constant in the news: הֶסְכֵּם שָׁלוֹם (a peace agreement).

w: בְּמַצַּב רוּחַ מְצֻיָּן|in high spirits|~lit. in an excellent state of spirit
s.line: and went back to their rooms in high spirits.
s.note: מַצַּב רוּחַ = mood: יֵשׁ לוֹ מַצַּב רוּחַ טוֹב (he's in a good mood), and אֵין לִי מַצַּב רוּחַ (I'm not in the mood).

s.line: Even Dorothy had hope that “The Great and Terrible Humbug,” as she called him, would find a way to send her back to Kansas,
s.note: A binyan pair: חָזַר (pa'al) = to go back, הֶחְזִיר (hif'il) = to send or give back: הֶחְזַרְתִּי אֶת הַסֵּפֶר (I returned the book). Dorothy's nickname echoes אוֹז הַגָּדוֹל וְהַנּוֹרָא. קִוָּה (to hope) gives תִּקְוָה, the name of the national anthem.

s.line: and if he did she was willing to forgive him everything.
s.note: סָלַח לְ־ עַל = to forgive someone for something; סְלִיחָה (sorry, excuse me) is from the same root.
